events.title: Growing resilience through community-led permagardens in Somalia: How women farmers are improving nutrition, food security and livelihoods with climate-smart agriculture
events.summary: Country: Somalia Source: Concern Worldwide Building resilient food systems at community level remains a priority across many of the contexts where Concern works. Yet establishing productive and sustainable gardens can be challenging, particularly in areas affected by climate shocks, water scarcity and limited access to agricultural inputs. In Somalia, Concern and its partner Lifeline Gedo have been addressing these challenges through the Irish Aid-funded Preventing Wasting in Madera Triangle (PWIMT) programme . Working through Mother-to-Mother Groups in the Gedo region, women farmers received training and technical support to improve soil fertility, manage water resources and grow diverse, nutritious crops using locally available materials and resources. Through community permagardens, participants applied climate-smart and agroecological farming practices to increase food production and diversify household diets. What is a permagarden and why does it matter? A permagarden is more than a vegetable garden. Drawing on principles of permaculture and bio-intensive agriculture, it is designed to maximise food production on small plots of land while making sustainable use of natural resources. Through techniques that improve soil health, conserve water and promote crop diversity, permagardens enable households to produce nutritious food that is available from production in the permagardens or accessible in markets from sale of surpluses throughout the year. (Image credit: NOAA Satellites) Download Image The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends November 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Nino. Below normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii. “NOAA’s unparalleled forecasting skill and scientific expertise provided the early warnings needed to protect lives and property this hurricane season,” said Neil Jacobs, Ph.D., NOAA administrator. “This included accurately predicting this year’s very strong El Nino months in advance, which gave us the critical insight we needed to accurately forecast this season.” Atlantic basin The Atlantic basin produced 10 named storms , of which one (Isaias) became a hurricane. Isaias was also the season’s only major hurricane with top sustained winds of 120 mph. An average season has 14 named storms (winds of 39 mph or greater), seven hurricanes (winds of 74 mph or greater), and three major hurricanes (winds of 111 mph or greater). Tropical Storm Arthur kicked off the season, forming near the Texas coast on June 17, which is close to the average date for the first named storm of the Atlantic season to develop.
